speechtext: In reply to the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Mutch) may I say that the question of parking has been receiving the attention of the Sergeant-at-Arms for some time. As hon. members know, there is only a limited space in the neighbourhood of the parliament buildings which can be made available for parking motorcars. The Sergeant-at-Arms has endeavoured to ascertain how many members have motorcars and wish to park them on parliament hill. There are officials of this house, for whom space has been reserved, who come here regularly, often they arrive earlier than members of parliament, and they are required to stay here very late at night. The question of parking on parliament hill is a problem, just as it is in every city. I can assure hon. members that the Sergeant-at-Arms is doing his best to provide parking facilities for all members. In view of what has been said today, I am satisfied that he will again go into this question.

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO SETTING UP OP COMMITTEE OF INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Kamloops asked me certain questions, of which I said I would take notice. I said I would get in touch with him in order to get the exact text. This I have done.
This morning the hon. member supplied me with information in which he pointed out that he had asked the following question:
The issue of the Montreal Standard on Monday contains the second instalment of an article "The case of Montreal missing gamblers." In this article it is alleged that Mrs. Balazo, the wife of one of the missing men, appealed to the Minister of Justice and the R.C.M.P. for assistance in tracing her husband and was promised an investigation would be made. That was in February. I would like to ask two questions:
(1)	If the R.C.M.P. made an investigation into the case, and if so, with what result?
(2)	In view of the allegations of the importation of American gunmen and of the existence of organized crime in Montreal and elsewhere, including counterfeiting and gambling, has the government given consideration to conducting an inquiry into the organized criminal activities in Canada along the lines of the inquiry which has produced such startling results in the U.S.A.?
It will be remembered that I answered the second of these two questions yesterday.
The answer to the first is that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were requested by the Montreal city police to publish particulars of the missing persons, Alex and Frank Balazo, in the R.C.M.P. Gazette, a publication which is distributed to all police forces in Canada. Stop notices were also placed in the R.C.M.P. fingerprint files in the event that fingerprint impressions of either of these men were later received.
Mrs. Alex Balazo wrote to the Minister of Justice on January 30, 1951, and asked if any assistance could be given in locating her husband. The letter was passed to the commissioner of the mounted police and was acknowledged by that official. At that time the item on these missing men had already been published in the R.C.M.P. Gazette, but a special notice was then sent to the large R.C.M.P. divisions instructing that investigators in the major cities be alerted in respect to this case.
I believe I should say also that the administration of justice, including the enforcement of the Criminal Code of Canada, by section 92(14) of the British North America Act is exclusively assigned to the provincial authorities, which create provincial and municipal police forces for these purposes.

The Royal Canadian Mounted Police provide certain national services which are available to all provincial and municipal forces. These include the police Gazette, the fingerprint bureau, and the firearms registration section. These services are used regularly by other provincial and municipal forces, and it will be noted that they were so used in the present case. Additionally, the R.C.M.P. are always ready to assist when requested by municipal and provincial forces; but if not requested they do not interfere in matters beyond their jurisdiction. Frequently the R.C.M.P. are asked by private citizens to investigate cases which are the primary responsibility of another law enforcement body, and in such instances they simply refer the inquiry to the proper police authority. In the present case, the R.C.M.P. took no action in or about Montreal, but merely used1 their machinery to circularize other police forces and their own personnel.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO SETTING UP OP COMMITTEE OF INVESTIGATION
speechtext: May I ask the minister whether the R.C.M.P. do not have a special responsibility with respect to counterfeiting, which perhaps would transcend the other jurisdictional boundaries he has described?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO SETTING UP OP COMMITTEE OF INVESTIGATION
speechtext: That is right. There are one or two exceptional cases of that kind, where the federal government is involved. There is counterfeiting, and then the same would apply where some major robbery took place in a federal department building, or something of that kind.

speechtext: Explain.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: EXCHEQUER COURT TO HAVE JURISDICTION IN ACTIONS ORIGINATING IN QUEBEC AND NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
The purpose of this bill is to free parliament from the necessity of processing individual divorce cases, a practice we all dislike, and at the same time to put an end to any agitation for the establishing of divorce courts in provinces where they are not wanted.
This bill does not establish divorce courts in Quebec or Newfoundland. It does not make available to persons residing in those provinces any facility not now available to them. It merely transfers the hearing of Quebec and Newfoundland divorce petitions from parliament to the Exchequer Court of Canada.
This is the same bill I have introduced on two previous occasions, except that it has

Inquiries of the Ministry
I have consulted the management of the Canadian National Railways, and the answer I receive is that if an employee of that organization joins a special force for a special purpose and for a specific length of time in a period of emergency, and is planning to return to his employment in the railway, he is protected as to his job, his pension and his seniority. Mr. Speaker, last night at 10.45 I rose to voice a grievance, namely, that the government of Canada has mismanaged the financial affairs of Canada and, more specifically, that the Department of Finance is failing to keep enough money circulating in appropriate hands to ensure the health of the body economic of Canada. To show that Canada's Department of Finance could better manage the financial affairs of Canada, I proposed to discuss two great monetary experiences of the last 140 years. The story of the first of these, the Guernsey island markethouse experiment, I summarized. May we turn now to consider the much more extensive experiment of the greenbacks of Lincoln's time in America?
The greenback was a unit of United States government created and issued currency, a debt-free dollar bill. Its use began in 1862 with the issue of $150 million of greenbacks to be spent into circulation debt-free. By 1863, $450 million of greenbacks had been issued and so spent. In June, 1864, there were outstanding $431 million of greenbacks. This money had all been spent into circulation for government purposes. A greenback was therefore a debt-free dollar when originally issued. The greenback was not supported or backed by specie. The greenback was legal tender for all debts except the payment of customs duties and interest on the public debt. For verification of these particulars see Sir Norman Angell's "The Story of Money" at page 293.
There were circumstances that would seem to make dangerous the use of the greenback by the United States at that time. When the new administration of Lincoln took office there were a number of serious financial disabilities, with which I shall deal briefly later on. The nation was engaged in a dangerous civil war, the outcome of which was by no means predictable. This fact would naturally result in public apprehension and pressure for increasing prices, inflation in our modem usage of the word.
Production in the United States was disrupted seriously because of at least two obvious factors. First, there was the relatively enormous number of men taken out of production to don uniforms and to engage in war industry, not to mention the horsepower taken out of production. Second, there was the considerable disorganization of normal commercial relations between the northern and the southern groups of states. Manifestly every degree of deterioration in the supply position of the northern states made goods

and services scarcer and resulted in rising prices, now called inflation, and constituting the only real inflation.
A whole nation accustomed to specie as the guarantor of the soundness of its money found itself suddenly absolutely upon a paper basis, with even its banks refusing, and being unable, to redeem either their own paper, or government paper, with any kind of specie.
The greenback was incessantly under attack from the money powers, as were the assignats, mentioned in my quotation from Robert McNair Wilson's "Monarchy or Money Power," to which I referred the other day, as reported on page 2525 of Hansard. To show the insidious part played by the United States bankers in opposing the greenbacks I should like to quote from the proceedings of our Canadian banking and commerce committee of 1934, at page 664. I quote from a statement by G. G. McGeer, the famous monetary authority, who said:
The national bankers' circular was issued by James Buell, the representative of the bankers' association in the United States, and a copy was sent to each banker in the States and it read as follows: "Dear Sir:
It is advisable to do all in your power to sustain such daily and weekly newspapers, especially the agricultural and religious press, as will oppose the issuing of greenback paper money, and that you also withhold patronage or favours from all who will not oppose the government issue of money. Let the government issue the coin, and the banks issue the paper money of the country; for then we can better protect each other. To repeal the law creating national banks, or to restore to circulation the government issue of money, will be to provide the people with money and will, therefore, seriously affect your individual profit as bankers and lenders. See your member of congress at once, and engage him to support our interest that we may control legislation."

A statement such as that may help hon. members to understand why they have heard only disparaging remarks about the greenbacks.
Then there was no form of price control in use by the United States federal government. The greenback was not subjected to intelligent control as debt-free money now could be, either as to the amount created, or as to the manner of spending it into circulation. There was besides no rationing or over-all control or direction of material supply.
What were some of the phenomena associated with the use of greenbacks? Opponents of debt-free money, state-created money, affirm that the greenbacks are unsound; that they caused enormous price

increases from an index of 100 in 1860 to 217 in 1865; that they hurt the wage earners whose wages during the same period rose only from 100 to 143; that those on fixed incomes, such as schoolteachers, were severely hurt; that soldiers were severely hurt; that the civil war cost the people of the northern states $389 million extra because they used the greenbacks.
But any kind of money, $450 million of it, spent by the government into circulation in the northern states in so short a period would have produced exactly the same rises in price. All we have to do is remember our own experiences in the recent war and in the first war. Specie borrowed directly from the United States banks would have done it. Currency borrowed from the United States banks or credit borrowed from the United States banks would have done it. Solid gold in the form of five dollar gold pieces stamped in the United States mint and spent by the government would have caused exactly the same price rise and created the same other effects, other things being equal. The rise of prices, therefore, could not with justice be blamed upon the greenbacks.
Fundamentally the price rise accompanying greenbacks was a result of having too few goods to buy with the greenbacks and all the other different kinds of money already in circulation. May I repeat that the price rise had and could have little or nothing to do with the kind of money the government used to spend, whether it was debt-free paper, debt or borrowed bank paper, paper backed by specie or gold in any percentage, coins of either silver or gold, either minted by the government and spent, or minted and borrowed from the banks and spent. A relative shortage of goods was the only monetary cause of the price increase. Of course, where there was no price control or rationing, price rises could have been the result of profiteering.
But there were several other contributing factors besides the spending into circulation of $450 million, no matter what kind of money those millions might be. Many weaknesses existed in the general financial situation prevailing at the beginning of the administration of Lincoln.
When the new administration of Lincoln took office, I quote: "it found the national finances in a very bad way". "The treasury was practically empty," "customs receipts had fallen off considerably," "the public credit was shaken," "the administration did not feel itself able to impose severe taxation on the people," and "three out of every four dollars the government spent was borrowed money." See "The Story of Money", pages 292 and 293.
Government Financial Policy
Soon after war broke out the government borrowed $150 million from the banks, demanding it all in specie, thereby weakening their specie position enough to force the banks off specie ultimately, and on to a strictly paper basis. Even at that the government had so little specie in its subtreasury that the government had to go upon an inconvertible paper basis.
Against this disquieting background, the government, sorely in need of funds, began issuing greenbacks. See Sir Norman Angell's "The Story of Money", pages 292 and 293. To recapitulate the adverse factors affecting the greenbacks: A dangerous civil war was unpredictable as to its outcome, thus engendering lack of confidence. Production was very seriously disrupted in the whole nation. The nation was accustomed to specie and so naturally was anxious about being only on paper. The greenback was constantly under attack by bankers and financiers. On the other hand, as I have already indicated, there was no form of price control. The greenback was not "subjected to intelligent control" as to amount created, or as to manner spent into circulation. There was no rationing of either retail goods or of raw materials for manufacturing. Finally, from any standpoint either of orthodox or of nonorthodox monetary thinking, the greenback was at a real disadvantage on the United States money market because of the fact that the government would not accept it in payment of customs duties and interest on the public debt.
Any just and accurate appraisal of the greenback experience must be made bearing all of these considerations strictly in mind; but when men talk of the greenback I notice they never bear any of these considerations in mind. They becloud their thinking.
What is the importance to us and our generation of state-created debt-free money? With it men can make financially possible what in a community is physically possible. This is a fact of epoch-making significance if men can only come to realize and appreciate it. If members of this house could come to appreciate that fact, it would mean the possibility of an epoch-making event in Canada, greatly to the benefit of this nation.
Let us now review the facts about Guernsey island. In Guernsey island the government in 1815 created and spent three thousand one pound notes with no gold or other backing except the going-concern-goods-and-services-producing-and-consuming-activi-ties of the island. These notes the government spent into circulation to build a markethouse from its resources, material and human, with the understanding that

Government Financial Policy those notes would be redeemed with revenues derived from renting the markethouse. Records indicate no inconvenient rise in prices. The state notes were therefore unquestionably sound money. The Guernsey islanders, therefore, built the markethouse at no financial cost whatever to themselves.
Did they get something for nothing? No. They merely set to work resources, human and material, that were not in actual use, and would have remained unused, except for the creation and spending of the state pounds. Before the government created and spent the three thousand state-note pounds, many of its workers were idle or partly idle. The stone in the quarry was idle. The tools were idle. Considerable food, clothing and shelter were unbought in the markets, and were therefore more or less idle or unused. Resources like soil and fisheries, ready to produce more food, etc., were partly or wholly idle. In other words it was physically possible for the islanders to build that markethouse. The physical potentialities of producing the necessary goods and services to build the markethouse were available to the islanders.
But they could not get the money essential to set those potentialities into action, to make their existing goods and services begin to be built into the markethouse, and then to turn such of their resources as fertility of soil, hay, milk cows, fish in the sea, fishing equipment, stone in the quarry, into replenishing goods and services, and to cause those additional replenishing goods and services, thus brought into being, to be built into more and more of the markethouse, and so on, until the markethouse would be completed.
The state pound notes, when created and wisely spent, provided the money essential to turn Guernsey island's physical possibilities of building the markethouse into the physical realities that constituted the completed markethouse. Therefore the Guernsey islanders did not get their markethouse for nothing. They built into the markethouse the requisite amount of stone from their quarry, their food, clothing and shelter up to that time being left unused, their human energy and skill up to that time unused. To effect the building process, to motivate it, they employed their'state-created one pound notes. In other words, they made what was physically possible, as regards a markethouse, financially possible as regards that market-house, by the use of the debt-free pound notes that the government created and issued.
Their markethouse cost them a substantial amount of depreciation of the stone in their quarry, of the fertility of their soil, and of

Debt-free money is the only means of scientific distribution. Hon. members will recall that men have solved the problem of production, but we must now solve the problem of distribution. Debt-free money is the key to the solution of the distribution problem. International plans such as the Colombo plan and others depend upon money. If you cannot or dare not obtain by taxing and borrowing enough money to finance Colombo plans, you cannot achieve your goal. With debt-free money and adequate production, men would be able to do all they desired to do with the Colombo plan.
Debt-free money, Mr. Speaker, used in conjunction with adequate production, constitutes the only possible means of preserving freedom, the only possible way of successfully combating communism.

GRUEN WATCH COMPANY V. ATTORNEY GENERAL OF CANADA   RETROACTIVE EFFECT OF 1949 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the grievance which I should like to raise this afternoon is one which, I regret to say, involves the good faith of the government in relation to assurances given on behalf of the government to the house and accepted by the house. The assurances in question were given to the house on November 30, 1949. The matter has to do particularly with a retroactive piece of legislation of the kind which parliament normally abhors passing and which it did not understand on that occasion that it was passing to have retroactive effect.
May I sketch briefly, sir, the background of this incident and the unhappy results which have flowed from it. On March 22, 1949, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) introduced his budget in the house. This was the famous pre-election budget. Among other resolutions introduced by the Minister of Finance was one to amend the Excise Tax Act in these words:
2. That the retail purchase tax be repealed and replaced by an excise tax of 10 per cent, payable by the manufacturer or importer, on all articles now subject to the retail purchase tax.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that prior to that time there had been a 25 per cent retail purchase tax applied to a wide variety of articles; and the purpose of this resolution, as stated by the Minister of Finance, was to eliminate that retail purchase tax and to substitute in its place a 10 per cent excise tax levied upon the manufacturer or importer. This would have involved amendments to sections 80 and 85 of the Excise Tax Act. But before it had an opportunity of dealing with that resolution, parliament was dissolved and a general election was held. In the meantime, however, even while these resolutions were being left suspended in the air-something that I hope will never again be allowed to happen during an election campaign-the government proceeded to apply these various changes contemplated by the resolution, although they had no legal authority whatsoever for doing so. There the matter remained, so far as parliament
Excise Tax
was concerned, until November 30, 1949, by which time litigation had been embarked upon by a number of litigants, arising out of the interpretation of this resolution introduced on March 22 and its doubtful meaning.
Just to fill out the history of the matter, I might add that on April 19 the government, acting under the resolution but without any authority from parliament, issued regulations purporting to define those to whom the new tax was to apply, listing instructions of a detailed nature with respect to the imposition and the collection of the tax.
May I now say a word, and I shall be brief about it, concerning the nature of the litigation which had been embarked upon in May of 1949. I shall not go into this matter in any great detail; there are technical questions involved. The essential point that I am making in giving this background information has to do with the way in which the rights of the litigants then before the courts of the land were treated by the government in this house and in subsequent actions.
As plaintiffs in the litigation there were certain importers of watches, watch movements and watch cases into Canada, these being in all cases finished articles. The practice was that the Canadian importer would purchase from the manufacturer abroad and would sell to the retail trade in Canada. These importers, of course, had not been previously personally affected by the 25 per cent tax because it had been levied at the retail level. When the resolution was introduced by the Minister of Finance in the terms in which I have quoted it, as you will recall, Mr. Speaker, it applied to a manufacturer or importer of goods as described in the resolution in the following terms:
-on all articles now subject to the retail purchase tax.
The litigation related to watches adapted in Canada to household or personal use. Briefly, the question in litigation was this. First of all, were these persons who imported the watches, watch movements and watch cases into Canada-so far as the putting of the watch movements into watch cases was concerned-manufacturers	or producers
within the terms of the resolution? If they were, did the new retail tax apply at the import level, payable at the time of import or at the time of sale by the importer to the retail trade?
There were important differences in the consequences that flowed from those two alternative interpretations; and one of the important consequences was that if the tax applied at the import level, these importers

Excise Tax
could not import apart from an import licence in the ordinary form of manufacturers' and importers' licence issued under the Excise Tax Act.
The interpretation put by the department on this resolution which, as I have said, was enforced for some months without any authority from parliament, was not an immediate interpretation. The resolution was not interpreted as applying to these importers for some weeks, but after the regulation dated April 19 was issued an attempt was made to apply the regulation to these particular firms, and they issued a writ in the Supreme Court of Ontario on May 7, 1949, seeking a declaration. I do not think that I need to dwell at length on the terms of the declaration they asked for, but briefly they asked for a declaration that they were not manufacturers or importers within the terms of the resolution, that the excise tax was not applicable at the time of import, and that they were entitled to import without the manufacturers' or sales licence.
The statement of claim in the action was delivered on May 23, two years ago today. The action was set down for trial on September 20, and was waiting trial, when the incident to which I refer in the House of Commons occurred on November 30, 1949. I do not dwell further on the issues in the litigation except to point out how entirely different were the two positions, the one being taken by the government, the other being taken by the litigants; the fact that these litigants seriously took their case to court, and that the action was well advanced and was simply awaiting trial when the question was raised in this house.
In the budget speech of the Minister of Finance at the second session of 1949, the Minister of Finance introduced new resolutions, and the resolution with respect to the Excise Tax Act amendment was similar in form to that introduced in the previous March. However, when the bill founded upon the resolution was introduced in this house questions were raised in committee of the whole following second reading. In the bill, which was Bill No. 175, which was before the house in the second session of 1949, amendments were proposed to sections 5 and 7 to amend sections 80 and 85 respectively of the act for the purpose of making the act clearly apply to such persons engaged in business in the way in which these particular firms were. There is no doubt that on the interpretation of the bill, it sought to amend the act for the purpose of making this tax applicable to these particular firms or persons engaged in similar business. Therefore

the question that arose in the house naturally was:	when will these new amendments,
amendments before parliament for the first time, come into force and effect? In the house on that occasion I raised the question, sir. It is to be found at pages 2503 and 2505 of Hansard of November 30, 1949.
May I remind you, sir, that the essential provisions designed to make the tax applicable to persons engaged in the manner I have described were sections 5 and 7 of Bill No. 175. When section 5 was reached I am recorded in Hansard as having said this:
Sections 5 and 7 are related for the purposes of the matter I should like to raise, which has to do with the imposition of an excise tax on the assembly of watches, clocks and certain kinds of jewelry. If I am correctly informed, this has become the subject of litigation as well as having been agitated by correspondence with and representations to the government. I understand that this litigation is pending and I am concerned as to whether this legislation will not cut right across the issues involved in the pending litigation which directly concerns the government.
Then the report proceeds, the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance being in charge of the bill at this committee stage:

Had I been trying the action prior to the 10th December, 1949,-

Chief Justice McRuer at the trial. In a moment I shall have occasion to refer to the recent judgment of the court of appeal. I continue:
Had I been trying the action prior to the 10th December, 1949, I would have made a declaratory order that the plaintiffs were not liable to pay excise tax in respect of the goods in question either on importation or on delivery to purchasers and that they were entitled to have such goods pass through customs upon payment of the lawful taxes then in force.
I also think that in such case the jurisdiction of the court should have been exercised to declare the regulations of the 19th April, 1949, ultra vires.
Then he refers to certain English decisions, and proceeds:
This peculiar right of recourse to the courts is a valuable safeguard for the subject against any arbitrary attempt to exercise administrative power not authorized by statute, and judges ought not to be reluctant to exercise the discretion vested in them where a declaration of the court will afford some protection to the subject against the invasion of his rights by unlawful administrative action.
Chief Justice McRuer went on to make it clear that, apart from this bill passed by the house on November 30, he would have given effect to the plea of the plaintiffs for the declarations which they sought. He would also have held that the resolution of March 22 introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) would have no application to the business carried on by these firms and, secondly, that the regulations issued by the Department of National Revenue in pursuance of that budget resolution which had no force or effect whatsoever, in law, were thus invalid and ultra vires.
But the defendant in the proceedings, the Attorney General of Canada, set up as a defence, if you please, the legislation which was passed in November, and in the very teeth of the undertaking given to the house to which I have referred, the undertaking given on behalf of the government that the bill then before the house would not apply to the pending litigation.

Excise Tax
The crown, as defendant, set up this legislation, this bill passed in November, as a defence in these proceedings. The chief justice of the high court, in the face of that, felt constrained to interpret that bill-contrary, I may say, to the understanding in the house-as applying to the pending litigation, and proceeded to hold that in the face of this November amendment he could not give effect to the plea of the plaintiffs in the action. That is the basis upon which his judgment proceeds, that the November amendment has application to the litigation before him.
Appeal was taken by the plaintiffs to the court of appeal of Ontario, and judgment was delivered on April 16, 1951. I might say briefly that the court of appeal in its judgment goes even further than did Chief Justice McRuer, in holding that the plaintiffs, apart from the November amendment, would have been entitled to everything they asked for. They would have been fully entitled to all the declarations they sought in their pleadings.
But the court of appeal felt its hands were tied by this November legislation which, contrary to the understanding in the house, and contrary to the assurance given to the house on behalf of the government, was then pleaded to defeat the rights of the plaintiffs in that litigation.
Now, everyone in the house who was present on that occasion accepted without question the assurance given by the parliamentary assistant on behalf of his minister, the Minister of Finance. If anyone in the house had had any question in his mind, after that assurance, that the bill could have any possible application to pending litigation, then certainly, had he raised the question, he would have been challenging the very plain statement and assurance given by the parliamentary assistant.
And yet-and here is where the bad faith enters into it, bad faith practised upon parliament, bad faith against subjects of the king in litigation pending in His Majesty's courts at that very time-notwithstanding those assurances given to the House of Commons; notwithstanding the interpretation put upon those amendments in the house when they were passed; notwithstanding the interpretation and understanding possessed by every member in the house, the crown, as defendant in the litigation, sets up this amendment as being applicable to that litigation- then pending, as having the effect of defeating the rights these plaintiffs had prior to the enactment of the amendment of November 30, 1949.

Sir, there was a time when the good faith of the crown was regarded as unimpeachable: it was accepted by all. It was the highest standard of good faith known in the land. But in these proceedings the good faith of the crown has been dragged into disrepute by His Majesty's advisers and representatives. By a deliberate government decision faith is broken with parliament. The statements made by the parliamentary assistant on behalf of the minister are soon ignored and, in effect, completely repudiated.
Counsel appearing in this case, on instructions of the Attorney General of Canada, simply acted-and could not do anything else -on the instructions given to him by the government, instructions which had the effect of reducing the assurance given in the house to the status of a scrap of paper.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a word or two on this matter because my name and the statement I made two years ago have been mentioned. The first point raised by the hon. member was the fact that the resolution was brought in in March, parliament did not actually adopt the resolution and the bill until November, and royal assent was not given until December. Of course that is the practice in this parliament. So far as excise tax changes are concerned, and for that matter so far as all tax changes are concerned, the night that the minister makes the budget address the tax changes are regarded as then being in effect. If parliament should later disapprove of the tax changes, then the people who paid1 the tax in the interval would

get a refund. If parliament confirms the tax changes then of course collection proceeds in an orderly fashion.
The British have a little different system. They pass a special bill to cover the gap between the introduction of the budget and the adoption of the bill. I well remember the incident, although not the details to which the hon. member referred, because between the introduction of the resolution in the spring and the actual passage of the resolution and the bill in the fall the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and one or two other hon. members, in whose ridings there are watch-making industries, raised this question. There was one particular case of litigation before the courts concerning a ruling of the taxation department as to whether or not the case and works if imported separately constituted the importation of a watch.
Because of the interest shown by members, the minister himself looked into the matter. I piloted the excise tax bill through that year as I have done in other years, and it was on the minister's instructions that I moved the amendment to which the hon, member has referred. Certainly I was acting for the minister and speaking for him. I must confess that I have not followed the court cases. I would not be expected to for two reasons. subtopic: SERVICE TO MONTGOMERY PLACE, SASKATOON
SERVICE TO MONTGOMERY PLACE, SASKATOON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too have a grievance that I want to air very briefly this afternoon on behalf of my constituents. Among the veterans housing projects is one which is in my constituency but is adjacent to and often considered to be within the city of Saskatoon, although it is just outside the city limits. These veterans were established there, built their homes under the Veterans Land Act, and settled there with their families. Of

Postal Service
course they required certain facilities including postal service. The matter was taken up with the Post Office Department, and as a result after two years of negotiation they were accorded the privilege of having their mail taken from the city of Saskatoon post office for distribution in the area known as Montgomery Place. I think I cannot do better than to put the correspondence on the record. May I say at once that if anyone raises a question about reading correspondence in the house, it is available to the house, and I shall be prepared to table it or do whatever is suggested regarding it. The first recent letter which has a bearing on the matter was written from Saskatoon and is dated October 23, 1948. It is from the office of the postmaster at Saskatoon and is addressed to Mr. G. Edwards, president, Montgomery Place ratepayers association, Saskatoon, Saskatchewan. It reads as follows:
Several months ago a request for postal services for the residents of Montgomery Place was received and forwarded to the Post Office Department for consideration. Although the total number of residents in the community is small-
I believe the number has grown since.
-the Post Office Department, following its policy of providing the best possible service to the people of Canada wherever feasible, has now arranged for a daily service to your community. On this inaugural day, on behalf of the Post Office Department I wish to extend to you and the residents of Montgomery Place our congratulations on the commencement of this new service. We trust that this service will prove adequate to your needs for postal facilities, and wish the community continued growth and prosperity in the coming years.
Yours very truly,
H. F. Hardy, postmaster
In other words, the representations of the veterans living at Montgomery Place were reviewed by the Post Office Department, obviously at Ottawa. After that review facilities were accorded and they were congratulated in the autumn of 1948 on the inauguration of this service. Everything went fairly well until a week or so ago. Then quite suddenly Mr. Tregaskis, who is now president of the Montgomery Place ratepayers association, received a registered letter reading as follows:
Dear Sir:
I have received a letter from the director of communications in which I am advised that our department is not prepared to continue payment for the mail service which has been in existence between Saskatoon city office and Montgomery Place. It appears that this arrangement, which has been in effect for two and a half years, is not in accordance with the general policy of the department.
The service was authorized in the first place through a misunderstanding or a lack of understanding in the department as to the whole situation, and it has been decided to discontinue this service.
[Mr. Coldwell.l
If I may comment there, when a service of this sort is requested and representations are made over a period of time, in this instance two years, surely the officials of the department should have no misunderstanding, certainly no lack of understanding of what the situation happens to be. I continue reading the letter:
Accordingly, Mr. A. C. Suffredine, the contractor for service between Saskatoon and Montgomery Place, is being notified today-
That is May 16.
-of the termination of the temporary arrangement under which he has been operating, to take effect at the end of the present month.
I have been asked to add that if the residents of Montgomery Place wish to have the service' continued and are willing to make suitable arrangements at their own expense, there will be no objection by our department. In any such plans which might be made by your association it would necessarily be understood that the responsibility of the Post Office Department would end with delivery of mail to the representative of your association at the city office.
Will you please advise members of your association at the earliest possible date.
Yours very truly,
L. S. Cumming,
District Inspector
In other words, two weeks' notice is given of the discontinuance of this service. If these people desire it continued they must pay for it themselves. Several post office matters of this description have been raised in this house in the past several weeks. I have always understood the post office was a service organization giving service to the citizens of Canada. Apparently just lately something has happened to the Post Office Department, and services that have been given are being withdrawn-I think I use the word advisedly in the light of this letter-arbitrarily.
Of course a protest has been made through the president of the ratepayers association. I might as well put that on the record too. It is dated May 21, 1951, and reads:
The Director of Postal Service,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Sir:
It was with great surprise that we received the attached copy of a letter from Mr. Cumming, the District Postal Inspector.
We would like to point out that it was with great difficulty that we obtained this service after two years of correspondence and interviews.
I know that to be the case, so there should not have been any misunderstanding or lack of understanding in the first place as to what this service involved. As I have said, I think the negotiations did cover a period of approximately two years.
When the service was instigated, we were of the impression that everyone concerned was very pleased to extend the service.

That would be indicated, of course, by the letter from the Saskatoon postmaster to the president of the ratepayers association of that day.
It would seem to us, that if there had been an error in supplying the service it should have been caught before two and a half years had gone by.
We hereby strongly protest the discontinuance of this service and ask that the matter be given further review with the circumstances of all concerned be taken into consideration, and a full explanation as to the reason that this service cannot be supplied.
The Montgomery Place Ratepayers Assoc., I. G. Tregaskis, President.
I may add that a copy of this correspondence was sent to me, and I see from the note on this letter a copy was also sent to the member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker). I believe this matter should be reviewed by the Postmaster General (Mr. Rinfret). I believe it will be reviewed favourably by the Postmaster General, because I think this is a case where a service was granted after two years of negotiation, where it has been in effect for two years and a half and is absolutely necessary to the people of the district. As the hon. member for Lake Centre will know, and the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) will know, this is in fact a suburb of the city of Saskatoon, although so far as parliamentary representation is concerned it is included in the constituency of Rosetown-Biggar which I have the honour to represent. I hope the Postmaster General will see that this situation is carefully and sympathetically reviewed. I believe that when he thus reviews it he will see the justice of the protest that is being made, and of the representations I am making in which perhaps other members will join me. That, Mr. Speaker, is the matter which I rose to deal with primarily, but there is one other grievance that I wish to bring before the house while I am on my feet. It will take only a very few minutes.
This concerns the matter raised by the member for Huron North (Mr. Cardiff) yesterday, cement. I listened to what the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) said, that he had no responsibility in that regard, but I believe the government should assume some responsibility. I am saying that because again today I had a telephone call from a small contractor just before I came to the house this morning who, in common with other small builders and contractors who have spoken to me or those associated with me, is unable to get supplies of cement.

Mr. Speaker, there is a matter that I should like briefly to bring before the house at this time, arising out of a development which occurred yesterday when it was announced that the express rates on shipments of fish from the maritimes to other parts of Canada-and I presume that this would apply to express rates on shipments generally-have been increased by amounts averaging up to 53 per cent of the rates prevailing only a short time ago.
This is a matter of particular importance to the fishing industry of the maritime provinces in general, and particularly in my own constituency where we catch and process a substantial quantity of fresh fish. I am not going to take the time of the house to emphasize the importance of this industry to the maritime provinces in general and to our own province in particular. I think the figures would substantiate the fact that approximately 35,000 people are engaged in this industry in the maritime provinces, not including the new maritime province of Newfoundland; and that last year the value of the fresh fish that was exported-that is, fresh and frozen-was over $33 million. Of that shipment, according to the figures of the Canadian National Railways, over 10 million pounds was sent to Canadian points by express.
That is a substantial quantity of fish moving in that way, although it is true that a larger proportion is hauled either by truck or by freight; and of course that is not affected by the increase. But there are particular advantages in express shipments of certain types of fish; and for those types, it is almost essential. This increase is going to weigh heavily upon the producers.
Unfortunately, despite the importance of the fish industry, as we all know the consumption per capita is not as great as we

should like to see it. The per capita increase in the consumption of meat, for instance, between 1939 and the present time was relatively great. I have the figures here, and I will put them on the record briefly. The consumption of meat then was 118 pounds per capita. That consumption has gone up now to 138 pounds per capita. On the other hand in the same period consumption of fish per capita has gone up only from 11-9 pounds to 12-3 pounds, a minor increase, despite the fact that the increased cost of production has been far less than the increased cost of the production of meat. This fact shows that there is a certain sales resistance to the marketing of this product, which has an adverse effect upon it.
There is no doubt in my mind that the increase in these express rates will adversely affect the sale of this product in the Canadian market. Although our consumption per [DOT]capita is low as a nation, we find that the farther one gets away from the seaboard, the lower that per capita consumption falls. For instance, in Halifax I believe we have a consumption of 35 pounds per capita. When you get to Montreal, that consumption falls to 17 pounds; when you get to Toronto it falls to 15 pounds; and, as I have said, the average for all Canada is less than 12 pounds per capita. An increase of 53 per cent in rates-[DOT] all the rates are not that high; the increases run from about 20 per cent to over 53 per cent-is going to result in one of two things. Either the consumer will have to pay more or the producer will get less. I do not think there can be any alternative to that whatsoever. If, as I have suggested, in view of the sales resistance, the consumer will probably not pay more, the producer will therefore be compelled to take less if he is going to remain in business. In other words one might say that this will be another indirect tax passed on to the producer and which he will have to bear. I am not at the moment criticizing the express companies for having increased those rates. They have, of course, to earn a profit on the business which they are doing. Possibly they can justify, or have justified, that increase, although I know that many suggestions could be made whereby they could reduce their tolls; but that is a matter which I think deserves the attention of the government.
This government and preceding governments have done a great deal for the development of the fisheries. This government today is spending thousands and perhaps hundreds of thousands on biological research, in development of processing, and in assistance in many ways. All that money is well spent. We appreciate it, but unless you can put your product on the market, sir, unless 80709-212J
Fisheries
you can maintain your markets, then those other expenditures are wasted. The money might just as well go down the drain.
The government, having the interests of the industry at heart, I suggest must do something about this new situation which confronts it at the present time. I have a statement which the Minister of Fisheries made some two years ago. The then minister of fisheries said this on May 5, 1949, in so far as the government's responsibility for the fishing industry is concerned:
This government over the next five years should take further positive steps toward the greater realization of the great fishery potential of the dominion. To help develop these resources and to expand the markets at home and abroad, the federal government should co-operate with the fishing industry in a program of development on the following lines.
I am quoting only one of them.
(a) for the industry as a whole the federal government should aid both in production and in the greater development of distribution, particularly in the domestic market.
Now, sir, this is a problem of distribution in the domestic market, and a problem which affects the future of this industry in so far as fresh and frozen fish are concerned. It is of tremendous importance to eastern Canada. The industry can grow and develop into a very vital economic factor-it is that anyway. It can develop into a still greater factor. Modem processing equipment and quality products, which are now being produced, augur well for the industry, provided that transportation facilities at a reasonable cost can be made available to the industry. I direct the attention of the government to that.
One other matter, Mr. Speaker, while I am on my feet, with respect to the fishing industry; this is a matter which I am sure has been directed to the minister's attention already. Within the last day or two resolutions have been sent to me concerning the effect of the operation of trawlers in the bay of Fundy and in St. Mary bay. The valley boards of trade, representing all the boards of trade in my constituency and I believe in the constituency of the hon. member for Digby-Yarmouth, joined in a resolution, the original of which was sent to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) or is in transit to him, and a copy of which was sent to me.
The situation there is a most serious one. In the old days, as you know, fishermen along that coast were fishing with hand trawls. They were what are called line fishermen. During the last two years there has been quite a development of the trawler. Everyone realizes that, so far as the deep sea fishermen are concerned, trawling is

Fisheries
absolutely essential. That is the only way in which you can get large quantities of fish, process them and bring them to market and maintain adequate supplies. But here we are dealing with inshore fishermen, fishermen who go out in little rowboats or motorboats two or three miles off their coast, fishing in inland waters. The operation of the trawler is an entirely different thing
You have two types of trawlers operating, sir. You have the large trawler, the deep sea trawler, coming into the bay of Fundy. There are American trawlers for example operating within three miles of our coastline; but sometimes their navigational aids apparently are in error, and they are found strangely enough close to the coastline, especially on foggy nights. They have been found within a hundred yards of the coast where they have been known to catch lobster pots. That was an error on their part, perhaps. Whereas our Canadian trawlers, operating with Canadian crews, financed by Canadian money, government assistance, are not licensed by this government except conditionally on their remaining twelve miles off our coastline, it is certainly an anomalous thing, Mr. Speaker, when United States trawlers, operating with United States crews and United States money, are allowed to fish within three miles of our coastline. The menace of the trawlers is such that we prohibit our own trawlers from operating within twelve miles. I presume that is a matter for negotiation with the United States government. It is a matter certainly on which some action should be taken.
Then there is the smaller trawler, the otter trawler, which operates under a different licence, and is allowed to fish anywhere near the shoreline. I see by the resolution which came to me this morning from the boards of trade that in the little waters of St. Mary bay, an inland arm of the bay of Fundy, 23 flounder trawlers were operating there the other day and five haddock trawlers, 28 trawlers in all in a little narrow arm of water, catching on the average around 8,000 pounds of fish a day, catching everything, big and small, with spawn and everything else, and each day throwing out hundreds of thousands of fish into the waters, which pollute the water, destroying the fishing beds and destroy the gear of the inshore fishermen.
The big haddock on the coastline of the bay of Fundy that come up there in the spring and summer to spawn and which go back in the fall have been caught for years by our hand fishermen, who thereby have been able to earn a reasonably good living. Now, all these fishermen are finding it extremely difficult to catch fish. The trawl-
[Mr. Nowlan.l
ers are capturing these fish by the thousand, and the hand-line fishermen who fish out of these little villages from Scotts bay right down to Victoria beach, in the constituency of the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis, are facing ruination unless some action is taken in the very near future.
I bring this matter to the attention of the minister and urge that, with respect to the operation of the large trawler, negotiations be entered into with the United States government to prohibit unconditionally their entry into the bay of Fundy. So far as the otter trawler is concerned, the small trawler, they should be relicensed, and licensed conditionally on their operating at least three miles off our coastline.

maintopic: INTERNATIONAL WHEAT AGREEMENT AND CANADA GRAIN ACT
INTERNATIONAL WHEAT AGREEMENT AND CANADA GRAIN ACT
speechtext:
shall take but a few minutes to bring a matter to the attention of the government. It arises out of the question asked today by, I think, the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) as to whether or not at the present session any amendments were to be made to the Canada Grain Act. The reply of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) indicated that such a possibility did not exist.
I rise for the purpose of bringing the attention of the government to two matters that are more or less connected with the question that was asked by the hon. member. On May 16 the question was asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), followed by a question by myself, which questions appear on Hansard at page 3077. The hon. member for Assiniboia said:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In view of rising costs of production and an increasing world price level, has the government made any attempt to have reviewed the present ceiling price under the international wheat agreement?
To which the Minister of Trade and Commerce replied:
The international wheat agreement is an agreement among some forty governments. It is now in its second year of operation, and the only action Canada could take to vary its terms would be to denounce it. Canada has no intention of denouncing it, nor has it any desire to do so.
Then the hon. member for Assiniboia added this question:
Could the minister not say whether any effort has been made to call in the countries and to talk it over?
No answer being given, I asked this question:
Without there being any repudiation of the international wheat agreement, could not the government

give consideration to communicating with the signatories to the agreement with a view to a revision in prices, having regard to increased costs?
Then the Minister of Trade and Commerce replied:
There are three producing countries involved in the agreement, and at least thirty-seven consuming countries. My hon. friend is optimistic if he thinks that the wishes of the three would prevail against the wishes of the thirty-seven. I presume that the signatories to the agreement would have equal standing in the agreement.
Having regard to the general attitude today in the western provinces, that under the international wheat agreement great losses will be suffered by the Canadian farmers unless there is a revision, that there has been a greatly increased cost of production to farmers, that the agreement is one which endeavours by anticipatory vision on the part of the government to determine conditions in the future, and that having regard to present world conditions, and the probability of those conditions continuing and bringing about a loss to Canadian farmers amounting possibly to hundreds of millions of dollars, something should be done now to secure a reconsideration of the basic prices laid down under the international agreement.
I realize that everything we might want cannot be secured upon request. But at least one would expect the government of the day to sound out the possibility of something being done under that international wheat agreement which does, in fact, contain a provision for periodical revision of price levels.
Yet the attitude of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) is simply one of brushing the question aside. There are only three countries which are producers, he says, and thirty-seven that are consumers; and he brushes aside as being impossible the success of any application on the part of the Canadian government for a rewriting of price levels. The international wheat agreement provides for a rewriting of the terms, and for periodical revision. Under that agreement, which will run until August 1, 1953, wheat this year brings $1.80 at Fort William to the Canadian farmer. It provides for the disposal of 500 million bushels of wheat, as follows: Canada is to supply 230 million, the United States is to supply 185 million, and Australia, 85 million.
I make the request of the government that it do something by way of endeavouring to secure a revision in price, in order to secure an increase in the minimum price, as at present set down in the agreement. Unless that is done this international wheat agreement will result in losses being suffered by the Canadian farmers beyond anything
Wheat and Coarse Grains we can comprehend at the moment. It is a serious question and deserves more serious consideration on the part of the government than for the Minister of Trade and Commerce simply to brush it aside by saying, in effect, "We have not done anything, because I do not believe that doing anything would secure any results."
I think the time has come for the Canadian government to point out the situation- for, after all, it controls, the wheat board, which in recent years has been its puppet for the purpose of carrying out government policy. I believe something can be done, with the international situation as it is today. Nations that are signatory to the international wheat agreement will realize that in the interests of our common defence, if for no other purpose, the producers in the producing countries should be assured a fair and reasonable price, or one more in keeping with present conditions than the international agreement provides.
Secondly I suggest that amendments are necessary to the Canada Grain Act. I say this because of certain facts which have come to light in connection with overages that elevator companies have been able to secure during the last few years. In the report of the wheat board, part IV, addressed to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and signed by the board, there is this paragraph that is of interest to every farmer in the prairie provinces. It states in part:
Deliveries to the board on the 1945-49 pool account totalled 1,435,955,510 bushels, of which 1,427,587,096 bushels were purchased from producers and 8,368,413 bushels were purchased from other than producers. The latter purchases represented principally country and terminal elevator overages purchased from agents of the board and for which no producers' certificates were issued by the board.
This means, if these figures are correct- and I believe they are-that the amount of the overages for which payment was not received by the farmers who produced the wheat in that period was 5,621,938 bushels.

the farmers have received no payment. I feel there should be an investigation into this matter, with a view to determining the situation in connection with this whole question of overages, and also thereby providing an investigation into the necessity for the making of amendments to the law, so that this situation, if found to be unfair and unjust, will be changed. For, after all, our concern should be for the, producer to receive the largest possible return for that which he produced.
Therefore, to sum up what I have endeavoured to place before the house, I would say, in two sentences, first that the time has come for the government of this country to rid itself of the nonchalant attitude exhibited by the Minister of Trade and Commerce regarding the international wheat agreement, and to have representations made to the other countries signatory to the agreement to the end that, having regard to the increased cost of production in this country, there will, in fact, be a revision of the basic or minimum prices provided by the international agreement. That should be done now. This is 1951, and the agreement has still two more years to run. Certainly it will be a matter of great enjoyment to those countries that will be paying less than they should be paying if they know in advance that the Minister of Trade and Commerce simply takes the attitude that nothing can be done even though no repre-. sentations have been made.
Then, secondly, in connection with the Canada Grain Act, I say consideration should be given to the necessary revisions of the act, if upon investigation it is found that the present system does not properly protect the farmer and assure him proper payment for his product.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCann (Minister of National Revenue) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 198, to amend the Customs Act.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Dion in the chair.
On section 1-Government vessels to report.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
This section provides that all the provisions of the act relating to certain things "are binding upon His Majesty in right of Canada or a province." This seems to be a rather unusual piece of legislation which is binding, not only upon His Majesty in the right of Canada but also upon His Majesty in the right of a province. The explanatory note reads:
The proposed subsection is new and is designed to make it clear that federal and provincial governments and their officers must comply with such parts of the act as are designed to give that control of import and export which is essential to the proper administration of the act.
This section purports to go beyond the ordinary tenor of a dominion act and provides that it shall be binding upon His Majesty in right of Canada or a province. While the minister is explaining that, will he explain also just what is the gap in the legislation that this is supposed to cover?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: There is nothing new in the principle of it affecting provincial as well as federal authorities. As an example, it might be applicable in seizures by provincial authority of liquor coming into the country. They would have to be turned over to a customs official for appraisal.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: Do I understand that this legislation undertakes to deal directly and not through the agency of provincial officials? Is that its effect?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: This is to enact that a provincial official is not free from the application of the law any more than any person else. It applies to provincial officials as well as to federal officials.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: We understand that all citizens are bound by any law passed here. The minister has said that this was not unusual, but can he give us an instance that it has been done before? I repeat, we understand that this law will apply to everyone, but it seems to me that the minister is going beyond that.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
This new subsection merely clarifies the law by placing beyond doubt the legal obligation on all persons, including officers of the federal or provincial governments, to report to customs when entering or leaving the country. The noncompliance with this requirement of government-owned vessels, through misunderstanding of the law, has made it advisable to propose this amendment.
There may be unusual circumstances where for reasons of emergency or convenience certain exceptions might have to be made and, as will be seen later, section 9 of the bill enables the governor in council to exempt from the regulations certain cases or classes of cases. An example would be the reporting by Canadian naval ships in time of war.
The second part of the subsection is similarly intended to make it clear that officers of the crown in the right of Canada or of a province must, like all other persons, meet the requirements of customs in regard to importation of goods, including flotsam, jetsam or wreckage.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: The minister has said that this is not unusual. Will ne give another instance where legislation goes beyond dominion officials and is binding upon provincial officials?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
Subsection 3 of section 2 of the Customs Act reads:
The rates and duties of customs imposed by this act or the Customs Tariff or any other law relating to the customs, as well as the rates and duties of customs heretofore imposed by any customs act or Customs Tariff or any law relating to the customs enacted and in force at any time since the first day of July, one thousand eight hundred and sixty-seven, shall be binding, and are declared and shall be deemed to have been always binding upon and payable by His Majesty, in respect of any goods which may be hereafter or have been heretofore imported by or for His Majesty, whether in the right of His Majesty's government of Canada or His Majesty's government of any province of Canada-

Section agreed to.
On section 2-Detention.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
I should
like to know something more about the acts which are referred to. The explanatory note reads:
The proposed subsection is new. A number of acts not administered by the Department of
Customs Act
National Revenue nevertheless contain clauses prohibiting under certain conditions import and', in some cases, export of goods of various classes. A customs officer while often directed by the act concerned to give effect to these prohibitions is under the section as it stands directed to release the goods immediately on payment of duty. The amendment will provide statutory authority for existing practice.
I should like reference made at any rate to some of the acts concerned, and I should also like an explanation of the statement that the amendment will provide statutory authority for existing practice. What has been the existing practice and what authority was there for it?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: As is indicated by the explanatory note, there are acts which permit importation or exportation of certain goods conditional upon their meeting specific standards or requirements laid down by other acts such as the Food and Drugs Act, the Fisheries Act, the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, the Seeds Act, the Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act, and others. In such cases the government department responsible for the act enforced by our officers is the logical final authority as to whether or not the goods in question comply with the specific conditions or terms of entry. To refer such cases to the competent authority requires the temporary detention of the goods, and all the new section does is to provide the statutory authority for that detention.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: What authority has ther been in the past?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: It is doubtful whether there was any authority. This would save the importer a great deal of trouble and perhaps expense if after his goods were declared they had to be seized and the duty assessed by another branch of the government which could act under its act, for instance, the Food and Drugs Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: I think I can see the reason for it, but what I am interested in is this. I should like to know a little more about it. The minister said a minute ago that it is doubtful whether there has been any authority. How long has that been in existence, and what kind of things have been done without authority? Have people's goods been detained without any authority of any kind, and how does the point arise now?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
The point arises because of the fact that the act says at the present time that on the importer paying his duty the goods must be released immediately. We contend that it would be advisable to detain the goods until such time as we have received information from the other departments concerned as to whether that type of goods should be admitted to the country.

Customs Act

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: Then do I understand correctly that the act has said that when the charges are paid the goods should be released?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: But notwithstanding that you have been detaining goods in certain cases because you thought, for the purposes of the other acts, it was the wiser course to follow. Is that correct?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: We try to co-ordinate one department with the other, and in some of the acts governing the importation of goods it says that they shall be held for examination.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: We have grown accustomed to orders in council, but is this a case where you did not even bother to have an order in council? Were these just minister's orders?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: It is stipulated in these other acts. For instance, the Animal Contagious Diseases Act specifically states that animals imported into this country must have a clearance from the authorities of the Department of Agriculture, which administers the act, before we are allowed to release them, even if the duty has been paid.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
But you
evidently feel that does not cover you because you are now passing this new legislation. I am just interested in knowing-and I think it is worth knowing as we pass

to what extent power is just taken in your stride, so to speak. We have often made complaints about orders in council but this seems to be a case where, as I said a moment ago, there was no authority of any kind, not even an order in council.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: There is a conflict of authority that we want to get away from. Our act as it stands says that goods shall be released immediately upon the payment of duty. Some of these other acts say that they shall be detained until there is a clearance from the particular department. In order to remove that conflict or repugnance, if you want to call it that, we are attempting to remove that difficulty by amending this section.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
I do not
imagine it is worth pursuing the matter very much further. I am interested to know why the minister speaks about a conflict of authority. I would not regard this as conflict
of authority. I would regard it as absence of authority, but I suppose we ought to be thankful that the minister is at last getting the power to do legally what he has been doing illegally.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-Goods otherwise exempt, dutiable in certain cases.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister a question with respect to this clause. It has to do with the collection of duty on goods brought into Canada for use by the armed forces or the government and their resale later. The effect of it is that, where a resale of goods is made to parties who are not entitled to import without paying duties, the duties shall be paid in full. Let us take a piece of equipment which is imported into this country and is used for two or three years. Is the duty payable on the depreciated value of the goods or on the cost value? I ask this question because I have been given to understand that a considerable amount of equipment was imported into Canada in this manner during the last war, and that when it came to pay the duty it was cheaper to ditch the equipment or throw it in a gully than to pay the duty, although there was still a lot of use in the equipment. Do the customs duties have to be paid on the original value or on the depreciated value of the equipment?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: The hon. member is entirely correct in his observation. When goods are brought in free or at a lower rate of duty, and then pass to other hands, the goods are dutiable in the hands of the new owner at the depreciated value at the time of the transfer.

Section agreed to.
On section 4-Overpaid duties not returnable after six months.
